Xi = CX2
where C and b are constants, the latter being negative.
I read only that short extract, Mr. Chairman. I do not know how widely this pamphlet is distributed. I propose to return to this matter when we reach the estimates of the Department of Agriculture. It may be that that pamphlet goes only to a few experts who are capable of understanding it, something which I am not capable of doing. It occurred to me that that is one of the things which happens when you feel that there is lots of money and that you can just spend your way through.
I now come to the details of the reductions and I ask the question: What principle was arrived at in reaching these reductions? Was it on the basis of necessities or luxuries? I shall just read a few, Mr. Chairman, and I hope I am well within the mark now. I will just read these few: Furs, electrical appliances, firearms, golf clubs; then I go on and I read: coin, disc or token operated games, ash trays, fountain pens, and so on. To refer briefly to one, namely furs: Are they a necessity or a luxury? The minister told us the other day, after a speech he had made in Toronto, that he had been convinced by a 83276-280i
Excise Tax Act
very eminent authority, namely his wife, that actually furs were necessities. However, I feel that that conviction arose after the budget and not before it. Now we come to firearms and complete parts thereof. I suppose they are used by two classes of people, namely sportsmen and gangsters. To gangsters I suppose they are a necessity but to sportsmen I take it that they are luxuries. And so it goes as we come to golf clubs, fishing rods and the others. My conclusion is that these results have been arrived at not on the basis of necessities or luxuries or on the basis of the greatest good to the greatest number but rather on the basis of the least good to the greatest possible number; in other words to spread it out as far as possible; in other words, to appeal to as many voters as possible. The principle seems to be the least good to the greatest possible number. That is the only principle that I have been able to discover in this list.
I should like to draw attention to one or two of the figures here; and when I am doing that I should like at the same time to draw attention to the increase in expenditure that has been going on. For example, let us take electrical appliances by way of illustration. We find that $5 million of the $33 million reduction is on electrical appliances. In passing I just point out that at the same time that is going on, the expenditure in agriculture proposed for this year is $76 million, roughly, which is up about $1,700,000. I come down to the small item of matches, which is $300,000. I mention at the same time that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation expenditure is to be up from $8 million to $23 million. I think there is a special reason there because I think a special earmarked tax, which we objected to a year ago, has yielded a good deal more than it was expected to yield. Therefore that figure-and I want to guard against any comeback on that matter-perhaps is, in a sense, accidental; but there it is. We have $15 million up there against a reduction of $300,000 that I just mentioned a moment ago. Then we come to candy and chewing gum. That is one of the large items-nearly $4 million-at the same time the expenditure of the transport department is up about $15 million. I do not think I need to take further time on this matter, Mr. Chairman. I just wish to point out that this microscopic $33 million reduction is all that we are getting to assist us at the same time that expenditures are going up, up and up.
I should now like to hasten to a conclusion. I should like to point out that we have to deal with these trivialities-because that is all they are-when big questions have received no answer. We are told on all hands that high

Excise Tax Act
costs of the things we produce may cause us great embarrassment in selling. Yet we go on collecting $1,200 million or more in corporation taxes. These taxes raise costs and make the difficulty of selling just that much greater. All that the minister has to say is to admonish the people who are in business that they must sharpen their pencils and do a better job. But no example is given by the government. I recall to my mind the words used somewhere in Shakespeare: "I could easier tell twenty what was good to be done than to be one of the twenty to follow my own good advice." I think that statement is true in the case of the minister.
We now have vivid, disagreeable and alarming evidence of the extent of unemployment because this very day we have had here representatives of the union of the unemployed. What a phrase that is that we have come to: the union of the unemployed. The union of the unemployed are here and yet nothing has been done. Nothing definite has been done with regard to unemployment. Indeed there has hardly been an admission by the government that unemployment is a serious problem. They are standing by and hoping that things will turn out all right. As I said a little while ago, it is the boom mentali ;y. We are relying on things improving in the United States, although that improvement carries with it no guarantee that our problems will be solved because as we know-and I shall not take the time to reiterate it again-the United States in many ways competes with us; and the fact that things improve there will not necessarily solve our problem at all.
The plain fact is that in the years that have gone by we have regarded boom as normal. We have bewitched ourselves into feeling that in some mysterious way because we have got a lot of natural resources we will always have a market for them. We are getting most unpleasant evidences from time to time that there is only a market for them at a price. We are getting even more disturbing evidences that we can be undersold in our own back yard, as somebody put it, by foreign manufacturers. As I said a moment ago, the mere fact that conditions in the United States may improve is no guarantee that ours will.
Therefore I should like to comment on this resolution. The reductions, even though it is very difficult to find any principle on which they were arrived at, will be welcomed of course by the people for whom they are made, but they seem to me to be without any rhyme or reason except the possibility of pleasing the largest possible number of people. It does seem to me that the upshot of it all is that we are just toying rather aimlessly with a serious situation.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I noted at the start of today's discussion on this resolution that it was referred to by the chair as "a" resolution. It is not my purpose to revive the discussions we have had in former sessions on a point of order so far as voting is concerned, but for the purposes of discussion may I ask whether we are discussing the whole of the Excise Tax Act resolution or whether we are discussing it clause by clause or paragraph by paragraph. The reason I ask that question is that the points I want to raise relate mainly to clause or paragraph 4 and perhaps some others. In other words, if we are taking the resolution paragraph by paragraph I am prepared to let paragraph 1 go, but if in order to make comments on paragraph 4 I have got to make them at this initial stage I will have to govern myself accordingly.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I think this matter was given a little consideration before we went into committee today. I consider that I am bound by the decision-I think it may be called a decision-of the house of April 26, 1951, which I think is summed up by the remarks of the deputy chairman found at page 2434 of Hansard of April 26, 1951. The deputy chairman said:
The hon. member was not in the house this afternoon when the matter was discussed as to whether or not the paragraphs of the resolution were to be discussed separately or as a whole. The decision was made by the house that they were to be discussed as a whole. Therefore what is now before the committee is not eight items or eight clauses. It is one resolution with eight paragraphs. Therefore there is only one item so far as the committee is concerned, and that is the whole resolution.
Accordingly, I think that I must permit discussion as members see fit upon anything which is included in the Excise Tax Act resolution now before us.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I will not ask you, Mr. Chairman, what you think of that course of procedure, if we have no alternative but to follow it. I wish to ask the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance a few questions relating more particularly to the sales tax or consumption tax which is included in this omnibus resolution. Can the parliamentary assistant say whether consideration was given to reducing the amount of the sales tax right across the board from its present total figure of 10 per cent to some lesser figure?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman. Certainly the budget is preceded by a great number of meetings between the finance minister, several of the other ministers concerned and their officials, and this is a development that takes place over weeks, even months. There is at all times an examination of the merits

in a particular year of making a tax reduction, if one is possible, in one section or another. My hon. friend of course realizes that the particular tax to which he refers, the 8 per cent sales tax and the 2 per cent old age pension tax, yields a large amount of money. As I recall it, I think the 2 per cent tax accumulated almost $150 million last year. Therefore a 1 per cent reduction in the rate of the consumption tax, as my friend describes it, on the same items that are subject to tax at the present time means a loss of revenue of something in the nature of $75 million. One can thus appreciate that a tax reduction of that amount in this particular year would have resulted in a forecast of a deficit.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I wish to express the view very briefly that it would have been better to reduce the sales tax right across the board than to remove the excise tax altogether from certain luxuries, as was done by the Minister of Finance in this budget. It does seem to me that the government is relying on the fact that people have become used to the sales tax and the government seems to have got away from any serious consideration of the possibility of reducing it substantially right across the board. In my view a 10 per cent hidden sales tax, that has as wide an application as this sales tax has, is a regressive form of taxation, and I regret that this year's budget did not include provision for a reduction in that sales tax.
May I now ask one or two questions under the general heading of the sales tax which relate to a more specific matter. Paragraoh No. 4 of the resolution before us includes a provision for repeal of the sales tax with respect to equipment sold to or imported by municipalities for their own use and not for resale, at a price in excess of $1,000 per unit, specially designed for use directly for road making, road cleaning or fire fighting, but not to include automobiles or ordinary motor trucks. That of course is a welcome relief to municipalities so far as it goes, but I suggest that its relief and its application are indeed very limited.
In connection with the position of municipalities, I should like to ask the parliamentary assistant to comment on the fact that the regulations under the Excise Tax Act, dated April, 1950, include this section numbered 12:
Where persons, firms or corporations produce printed, multigraphed or mimeographed matter for their own use, to a value of over $3,000 per annum, they are required to account for the consumption or sales tax on their total production of such goods. The tax is to be computed on the total cost of all materials, including electros, engravings, stereotypes, plus 220 per cent. The value of negatives, electros, engravings, stereotypes, half-tones, and other printing plates is to be included only once-
Excise Tax Act
That is very kind of them.
-in the value on which sales tax is to be calculated and not each re-run.
This regulation was drawn to my attention by one of the officials of my own city of Winnipeg. In drawing this to my attention it was pointed out that from my own experience, having once upon a time been a member of the council of the city of Winnipeg, I know there is a need for mimeographing a great deal of material so that it may be placed in the hands of the aldermen and others who have to work on it. It has been pointed out to me that if in preparing this material the officials simply used typewriters and sheets of carbon paper so as to produce carbon copies, they would pay only the 10 per cent sales tax upon the cost of the typewriter ribbons and on the cost of the paper and carbon paper that would be used. Obviously when a great many copies and a good deal of material has to be prepared that is a rather inefficient and expensive way to do it. The officials of the city of Winnipeg, therefore, like the officials of other municipal bodies, resort to the use of mimeographing machines.
But lo and behold, this regulation under the Excise Tax Act makes the provision that I have just read. It works out this way. If the city council of Winnipeg purchases mimeograph paper worth $1,100 and simply leaves it on the stock shelves the only tax that would be paid would be the 10 per cent tax. But if it is used for its own purposes, namely for the production of mimeographed documents, it works out this way. The sales tax item of $100 is first of all reduced, leaving the value at $1,000. But then there is added to that $1,000 for the purpose of computing the sales tax the amount of 220 per cent, so you add $2,200 to the $1,000 which gives you $3,200 as the figure on which the sales tax must be computed. It is then that the 10 per cent figure is brought into play, and 10 per cent of that amounts to $320. This sales tax of $320 has to be paid on an original purchase of $1,000.
When I started to give this example I believe I said we should assume the purchase of $1,100 worth of mimeograph paper. What I should have said was, assume the purchase of $1,000 worth of mimeograph paper plus the 10 per cent sales tax which would bring it to $1,100. It is from that point the deduction of $100 is made so that the much larger figure can be added. The result is, as I say, here is a sales tax of $320 that has to be paid on a purchase of $1,000. I do not believe the aldermen of the city of Winnipeg are particularly incapable of understanding things, but it looks to them as

Excise Tax Act
though they are paying a 32 per cent sales tax on their mimeograph paper and mimeograph supplies.
When the Winnipeg officials have taken this matter up with the authorities to try to get an explanation, they have been given the explanation that if they had the material printed the sales tax that would be paid on all the plates and materials that went into the printing process would result in their paying a figure which would come to that amount. Surely a city council is not going to be asked to compare the mimeographing that has to be done for its regular meetings or for meetings of its committees, which has to be done very quickly and in many cases is just for temporary use, with the kind of material it is necessary to print in more permanent form. As has been pointed out to me, the whole purpose of resorting to the mimeograph process is to do a job that would normally be done not by printing at all but by the typewriter and by the making of carbon copies. It is an attempt to be more efficient and more economical that leads to the use of the mimeograph process rather than typing carbon copies.
The figure I have for a recent fiscal year in the city of Winnipeg suggests that the amount of tax that has to be paid is not going to break our city of Winnipeg. As a matter of fact it is the sum of $1,254.78. But it does strike the aldermen of the city of Winnipeg as a rather large sum to pay in taxes on mimeograph paper, especially when for all practical purposes it works out to a rate of 32 per cent. I should like to have the comments of the parliamentary assistant on that situation. I can hardly ask him to justify it, because I do not think it can be justified. I suppose he can give the explanation for this gouge, if I may call it that, that has been given to the city of Winnipeg, but more particularly I should like to know whether consideration has been given to the eliminating of the regulation which I read so there will not be this sales tax of 32 per cent on mimeograph paper and supplies.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I confess that the detail on this point is new to me. But I know the hon. member holds a card in the printers union, and he doubtless appreciates that any printing of this kind on a large scale, we will say in an industry or something of that kind, is to that extent in competition with the printing that would be done in the normal way by the printers and bears a considerable labour content. From the remarks he made, I was not quite clear whether he felt that a regulation of this kind should be removed solely in respect of municipalities, because he started his discussion with reference to an item in the resolution dealing with municipalities.
Is the hon. member saying that if the expenditure were over $1,000 in the case of a municipality, this particular requirement should be waived? Is he saying that any business firm or anyone else with internal printing of that size should also escape the imposition of this form of tax?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: In reply to the first comment made by the parliamentary assistant, may I remind him that I dealt with it before he made it. I pointed out that this is not material that would otherwise be printed by any letter-press process, or even by an offset process, but it is material which would otherwise be produced for the aldermen by the process of typing carbon copies. There is no element here of competition with the established printing trade.
Would it be mimeographing?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Yes, that is what we are talking about, the mimeographing of reports, agendas and things of that sort that you have to have around the city hall, most of which material is not of a permanent character. I know quite well that the minutes and proceedings of the city council of Winnipeg, which are permanent, are printed. Indeed they are printed in a union shop, I might tell the parliamentary assistant.
As to the other question, it is the government that boasts, as the minister did when he presented his budget on April 6, that it is doing something to relieve the costs imposed upon municipalities by taxation. If the government wishes to go further with this matter and establish some figure at which exemption would be granted, that is up to the government. I confess I am not as much concerned about the relief of taxation as it would affect private firms in business to make money as I am about the relief of municipalities who operate wholly on the basis of money they receive from the taxpayers, and mostly on the basis of money raised from taxes on real estate. I have tried to answer the question of the parliamentary assistant, and I would be glad if he would answer mine.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Frankly I do not think that in all cases my hon. friend could assure anyone that only mimeographed paper would be used, and that the machines being used internally could not be of another type- perhaps of the offset type-which might be in direct competition with a printing plant. As I said at the beginning, it was a new point so far as I was concerned. Certainly I shall make inquiries about it; but I was
(Mr. Knowles.]

anxious to find out whether my hon. friend's concern was solely from the point of view of the municipalities.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is my chief concern.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes. It is not one of those items that is particularly spelled out in this resolution. I still disagree with the hon. member when he suggests that another municipality, for a completely different purpose, other than that of minutes, could not probably use another type of printing.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The government itself, under the terms of paragraph 4 in the resolution, has accepted the principle that municipalities are entitled to some relief from the sales tax.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes, on some things. This is the first step. We are going reasonably cautiously with it. We have always explained in the past that we feel a great many municipalities have to be dealt with. Administrative difficulties are sometimes heavy in proportion to the expenditure. All those things have been explained in the last two years. This is the first step of its kind. The hon. member makes reference to a rather unusual item that he thinks should be added. He will recognize of course that I am not in a position to say that it can be added this year. I can assure him however that his remarks will be considered by those who will be looking into the matter at a later time.

I have a question referring to paragraph 4(c) which, as has been noted, assists municipalities in carrying out their functions by giving some relief from the sales tax. It refers to certain items of equipment. A good deal has been said in the general debate on the budget as to the problem of the municipalities under the present division of taxing authority or taxing power. It has been made apparent that they are being heavily subsidized by the provincial governments to enable them to carry out their responsibilities. I note that in the case of provincial governments the sales tax is given as a complete exemption in the articles with which they have to deal, and that the principle has also been extended to public hospitals and other institutions by way of assisting them in carrying out their purposes. As the parliamentary assistant has said this paragraph represents the first step in one method of assisting the municipalities. I know, too, that we have on the order paper item No. 9 the import of which is not yet known to us, but which is as follows:
Resolved, that it is expedient to bring in a measure to extend the benefits of the Municipal Grants Act and to provide for certain changes in connection with the administration of the act.
Excise Tax Act
I assume that this is a measure to assist municipalities by federal action. The fact that this appears on the order paper, and the further fact that a brief, which I have seen, has been submitted from Toronto, a city of which my riding is not an inconsiderable part, leads me to ask the parliamentary assistant whether he would care to indicate whether the government has set its face, shall I say, against any additional exemption from sales tax for the municipalities. In other words, is it going the whole way in freeing them from this tax and, if so, whether this other method of assisting the municipalities, which is not yet known, is in any way comparable in extent?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: This is as far as the government intends to go in this field at the moment. My hon. friend has referred to other legislation which, I may point out, amends an existing statute so as to make it more generous. I would remind him that the original legislation is relatively recent. It is only in recent years that the federal government has made grants in lieu of taxes to municipalities. As I say, this is new; and after consideration prior to the budget this year this is the extent to which the government will go.

There are some good things in paragraph 4. Those who suffer from failing hearing will now get their equipment free of sales tax. In the last three years the minister has been asked to free hearing aids. This is the first time it has been done, and it is important to many people. It may not seem important to some, but those who are selling hearing aids believe it is. And I am sure those who buy them will share that view. I commend the minister for having taken this step as set out in paragraph 4 (g).

Could the
minister give figures showing the loss of revenue in respect of the item set out in paragraph 1 of the resolution.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I could give an estimate. The revenue loss estimated for the coming year in respect of electrical appliances is $5 million. I believe that was the figure used by the hon. member for Greenwood. The estimated loss of revenue in respect of furs is $4,400,000; coin operated merchandising machines, $250,000; cameras, $1,350,000; firearms and ammunition, $1,300,000; fishing rods and reels, $350,000; golf clubs and golf balls, $200,000; luggage including trunks, bags and the like, $3,300,000. Those are the items in respect of which the entire 15 per cent is being removed.

Excise Tax Act

I have a question on some of the other items in part 2. This was brought to my attention by a man who is in the undertaking business. Line 4 reads:
. . . for use in connection with the care of the human body.
Down below that it says:
Preserving or restoring.
He wondered whether that included embalming fluid.
Paragraph (d) reads:
Coin, disc or token operated games or amusement devices of ail kinds.
Does that include those machines of chance?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No; a distinction has been made between vending machines-
That is in No. 1.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The hon. member is referring to No. 2?
Yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Only the 5 per cent reduction applies to that type, and the 15 per cent applies to the vending of merchandise as opposed to or contrasted with the use of the machine for amusement purposes.
There is no deduction on the machine of chance.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Five per cent.
Five per cent only?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes. Everything in item 2 is subject to a 5 per cent reduction, bringing the excise tax from 15 per cent to 10 per cent.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Does that apply also to machines that are illegal under the Criminal Code?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am not aware of that kind.
I believe they are included in this 5 per cent reduction.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: A fine example of cabinet solidarity.

Paragraph (e) of No. 2 mentions pipes, cigar and cigarette holders and so forth. Was any consideration given to reducing the tax on cigarettes? The reason I ask that is that in this morning's paper the Royal Canadian Mounted Police report that they caught two men smuggling
165,000	United States cigarettes, and another case of 140,000 cigarettes and another two men were arrested with 25,000 cigarettes. It is all in this morning's paper. With the tax on cigarettes in Canada as it is at the

present time we cannot expect anything else but that people will try to smuggle them in. I ask the parliamentary assistant whether any consideration was given at this time to this matter.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: A very substantial reduction was made last year, partly having in mind the matter of smuggling which had been increasing. We believe from the evidence in the intervening period of the past year that this kind of thing has gone down very considerably since the reduction of last year.

It is still pretty high, though, which I believe the assistant to the minister will acknowledge. In paragraph (i) of item No. 2 we find that the tax has been reduced on clocks and watches. Clocks and watches are an absolute necessity. Although this will help the Canadian industry to some extent, I do feel that some restraint should be put on the import of parts of watches because it will certainly ruin the Canadian trade. In paragraph (j) of item No. 2 we find:
Articles of all kinds made in whole or in part of ivory, jet, amber . . .
And so forth. Practically everything that is mentioned in this paragraph is imported. Is this change made to help the importers? The stuff is not made in Canada; most of it is imported into Canada. A reduction from 15 per cent to 10 per cent is made on articles made of ivory, jet, amber, coral, mother of pearl, natural shells, tortoise shell, jade, onyx, lapis lazuli, or other semi-precious stones. All that stuff is imported.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I think the hon. member for Peterborough will recognize that a number of these items are reassembled into other articles of jewelry and adornment and the tax reduction, added to the reduction in the general classification of jewelry, will doubtless be reflected in the ultimate consumer price.

Just one more question. Item No. 7 reads:
That provision be made to ensure that machines and tools for operation by tractors are not included as accessories therefor in the prevailing exemption from sales tax.
With respect to tools and machines for operation by tractors, there would be hydraulic lifts, shovels, blades and different things of that kind. Can the assistant to the minister tell us just what is meant by this item?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
At the present time the act provides for an exemption for tractors for farm purposes, or used for logging, and accessories for this purpose; but some items are

not considered to be accessories for which the exemption is intended: Such things as bulldozers and tractor shovels, tree dozers, cable control units, hydraulic control units and things of that kind are not to be considered as accessories entitled to the exemption.
A hydraulic lift on a tractor is almost a necessity on some farms, because the farmers have to use them all the time in handling some of their equipment. Why should they not be included in it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: An item such as my hon. friend describes, and particularly the ones that I recited, are considered rather to change the function of the tractor itself. It gets you into a different field, and they are not considered to be accessories.

Can the parliamentary assistant give me the estimated total tax loss which this resolution will cost and also two or three items which I should like to have the details on. First, paragraph (h) of item No. 2, tires and tubes, and, second, the item to which I referred before, namely, equipment for municipalities. How much is estimated will be lost on these two items and on the whole resolution?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Really, Mr. Chairman, we have not a good estimate on the possible revenue loss in connection with the exemptions on certain items for municipalities. The exemption does not apply to all municipal purchases for which there might be some statistics. I am afraid I could not answer that particular part of my hon. friend's question. I can give an estimated loss of revenue on the reduction of excise taxes on certain articles from 15 per cent to 10 per cent. On tires and tubes, which the hon. member asks specifically, the estimated loss is $3,500,000; candy and chewing gum, $3,950,000; fountain pens and pencils, $275,000; jewelry, glass, china and those other items, $2,400,000; lighters, $100,000; matches, $300,000; motorcycles, $50,000; slot machines, $100,000; smokers' accessories, $150,000; soft drinks, $3,800,000; toilet articles, $2,800,000; carbonic acid gas, $100,000.
Can the parliamentary assistant give an estimate for the whole resolution, if only approximate? There must be some estimate of it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The major items are in paragraphs 1 and 2 and each amount to about $16 or $17 million, and I would suggest the average would run to about $36 million.
That is true probably of the entire forecast?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Yes.
Excise Tax Act

I would like to question the parliamentary assistant with regard to section (c) in paragraph 4 which deals with the deduction with regard to municipalities. It seems to me there are quite a number of conditions surrounding that expenditure in excess of $1,000 in regard to equipment used directly for road making, cleaning, or fire fighting, but not in the case of automobiles or ordinary motor trucks. As one looks at this amendment to the Excise Tax Act it seems to be somewhat of a gunshot prescription. There does not seem to be any particular justification for reductions on some articles while others are left as they were.
For instance, in this section we have a reduction on mink coats, fishing rods, and golf balls, but we have a limitation on the reduction as it affects municipalities which are hard-pressed at the moment. It appears to me as though the government is trying to do something for the municipalities and is then undoing it. Surely automobiles and ordinary trucks are used for fire fighting, road maintenance, road cleaning and so on. The hon. member for Peterborough has also raised the question of accessories on certain equipment used on the farm which is almost as important today as the tractor itself, and I am rather amazed that more consideration has not been given to such items.
This' is a very tardy way of handling tax reductions in any event. The entire tax reduction proposals are minor in character. In fact the government will be taking more from the people this year than they took last year while ordinary expenditures have increased. You cannot very well call it a substantial reduction in taxation if you merely take a little bit off mink coats, golf balls, fishing lines and a few other things and leave the same tax on the attachments to farming equipment. The farmer uses these attachments such as manure and gravel loaders, and they are as important as the tractor.
When we turn to the municipalities, on whose behalf we have been pressing for reductions for a long time, we find the government will allow them a reduction on anything over $1,000 but not in the case of ordinary motor trucks or automobiles where no reduction is allowed at all. I would submit, Mr. Chairman, that an ordinary motor truck is essential for fire fighting. It is essential for road cleaning and maintenance. I would like the parliamentary assistant to give us the reason why we have these fancy, delicate reductions in the case of luxury items while with other things which are an absolute necessity in carrying on municipal functions there has been no reduction at all.

Excise Tax Act

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: An attempt was made in taking this step for the first time to include a number of the more costly items on which municipalities obviously must spend a substantial amount of money. The question of exempting motor vehicles was certainly looked at but, on the other hand, it was felt that in the treatment of some of these major items of municipal equipment there was much greater likelihood that they would be subject to resale and trading and that would have a greater effect on the general automotive truck and automobile business.
You mean up to $1,000?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No, over $1,000.
But you mean there would be more trading up to $1,000?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: An automobile would probably be put on the market again for resale much more readily than other things, particularly if it had a lower tax rate than was general within the community.

Mr. Chairman, on paragraph 4 I would like to draw the attention of the parliamentary assistant to a request made by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture to which I referred earlier in connection with stock feeds. Perhaps the best way in which I could do that would be to read the submissions of the federation which are contained in a brief submitted to the department. This is their statement:
In dealing with the Excise Tax Act, we requested that all materials used in the manufacture of stock feeds be made exempt from sales tax by adding the following item to the farm and forest section: "material to be used exclusively in the manufacture or production of poultry, cattle and other stock feeds" and that the following item be added to the tax exempt farm and forest list of schedule III of the act; "antibiotics and veterinary drugs."
Apparently nothing has been done in that direction as far as I can judge, and at this time I would ask the parliamentary assistant to bring this matter to the attention of the minister so that it might be given some consideration. Obviously we are not going to pass all these resolutions today. I would be quite happy to move an amendment in this regard, but, of course, it would be out of order under the rules of the committee so I will content myself with the hope that the minister will give that request consideration. In my estimation it is a reasonable and modest request and there seems to be no reason why materials used in the production of livestock should not be treated in the same manner as other farm equipment which goes into the cost of production. I hope the parliamentary assistant will give this matter some consideration.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Consideration will be given to the hon. member's remarks. I recall that he did refer to this brief in making his speech on the budget but I would draw to his attention the fact that under the schedule in the Excise Tax Act there are quite a number of categories given exemption and they include a long list of foodstuffs and a long list of farm products. In so far as stock feeds are concerned they are not subject to a sales tax, but it may be that certain items that are part of the mixture are themselves taxed because they have been manufactured somewhere else. Stock feed, which is the finished item, is a compound of the whole thing and not subject to tax.
Of course that is a reference to the materials used in the manufacture of stock feeds, and is quite a different matter.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the parliamentary assistant a question. Section (h) of paragraph 2 mentions tires and tubes in whole or in part of rubber for self-propelled machines or automotive vehicles of all kinds. I suppose that includes bicycles. Could the minister tell us how many of those tires and tubes are imported? The reason I ask is that I was in a store last week and they did not have a Canadian tire in the place. They were all imported tires and it appears that they can get them cheaper than from Canadian manufacturers.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I have not got that figure for my hon. friend at the moment but I will make a note of his question and see that he is supplied with that information if it is possible to obtain it.

I would like to ask the
parliamentary assistant if the tires included in the purchase of a new car are exempt from this tax.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes.
And when the manufacturer buys tires to put on combines or farm machinery or trucks does he get that exemption?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: They are considered to be an accessory in the case of farm machinery and come under the general classification of, I believe, section 409 of the Customs Act which covers the free entry of farm implements.

I should like to ask the parliamentary assistant a question. I did not quite clearly understand him when he mentioned the fact that bulldozers and road equipment

are exempt. It is understood that under paragraph 4, clause (c) to which I had referred, bulldozers and road equipment would be exempt from sales tax?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: My hon. friend and I are really not referring to the same section. I think that in paragraph 4 (c) there is a list of equipment on which municipalities will no longer have to pay sales tax.
Oh; I see.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The discussion in connection with bulldozers had reference to another item in this resolution.
That is what I thought.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Bulldozers, if over $1,000 and purchased by a municipality, would not be subject to sales tax.
For information purposes only may I ask this question? As to a bulldozer that is purchased for logging operations or for farm operations, is it exempt from taxation?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
That is correct; in a
general way.
In a general way?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: As you know, there is the matter of from the stump to the common carrier; I think that is the general phrase used in logging operations.

The tax is on for construction companies; on bulldozers purchased by these companies there is a tax but for a farm operation or for making bush roads and so on, bulldozers and other machinery are exempt, are they not?
A bulldozer is not exempt on a farm.
Maybe your farm does not need a bulldozer.
Yes, it does. That is why I asked about hydraulic equipment.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No. I am informed that in the case of a logging operation-that is the pushing out of the road-the bulldozer would bear tax.
It would bear tax?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes.
Nearly all other types of logging equipment are exempt, are they not?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Yes; generally speaking. There is a classification like the farm implement classification.
Excise Tax Act

In logging operations bulldozers are extremely important machines. Neither the provincial government nor the dominion government assists companies and loggers much in building roads which are helpful for fire fighting and are also absolutely necessary for the carrying on of their operations.
I might submit that I do not think there is any other item in logging operation equipment on which the exemption would be more greatly justified than it would be on the bulldozer. As the parliamentary assistant indicated a few minutes ago this afternoon, I realize that there has been a certain amount of caution and a certain amount of fear that some of these articles would be juggled, where advantage would be taken of the exemption and they might be resold or retraded. There may be administrative difficulties along that line but I wish to submit to the parliamentary assistant and his minister that serious consideration might be given to the exemption of bulldozers, machines which are of such great importance in production.
Again I want to emphasize the fact that it is highly desirable that roads should be built through the forests for the purpose of fire protection. I have often suggested that both provincial and dominion governments should co-operate to a greater extent with operators in order to get a better system of roads for fire protection and for the development of proper forestry through the various northern sections and areas that are not being operated effectively, in order to protect the trees from disease, fungi, fire and so on.
I just wish to draw this matter to the attention of the parliamentary assistant for his consideration. As everyone who is familiar with bush operations knows, in the matter of building roads a bulldozer is just about as essential as is any other implement in that field. I think some reconsideration might be given to this matter.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: So far the exemption is limited just to the tractor portion of the equipment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have no objection to the resolution carrying today, if that is the wish of the committee; but there is one other subject that I want to say something about. However, I am prepared to do it on second reading of the bill. Since I have indicated that there is such a subject, perhaps I should let the parliamentary assistant know what it is so that whoever is piloting the bill through the house at the second-reading stage might be prepared to discuss it. I refer to the request of charitable

Excise Tax Act
organizations for a sales tax refund similar to that which is granted to hospitals. Whoever is sponsoring the bill on that occasion can find what we will probably say by looking at Hansard of March 31, 1953. There the parliamentary assistant will find that his colleague the hon. member for Spadina as well as the hon. member for Eglinton and I spoke on the question. I am sure that the other members to whom I have referred will agree with me that the time has come for something to be done in this connection. We shall have more to say about the matter later, in case it is the desire of the committee to pass this one resolution today.

I do not want to hold the
resolution up, Mr. Chairman; but before it passes I should like to have some assurance that the parliamentary assistant and his minister might give some consideration to paragraph 4 (c) with reference to municipalities. I do not want to hold the resolution up beyond six o'clock, but I still feel we have not been given any real reason why the exemption is limited to articles whose price is over $1,000 or why a motor truck should not be included as a necessity for municipalities, for such purposes as road cleaning, road construction and so on. I cannot help thinking that the government might well have considered these articles and might not have so greatly restrained their reductions. As far as I am concerned, I will be satisfied if the minister would agree to give serious consideration again to that item. I do not want to hold up the resolution.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Fairly serious consideration has already been given but it certainly can be reconsidered between now and the time of bringing in the bill.

I do not want to hold the resolution up either, Mr. Chairman, but I do not feel altogether happy about the answers we have been getting, as I understand it, as to why this reference in paragraph 4 (c) "in excess of one thousand dollars per unit" is necessary. As I understand it, the suggestion has been made that it would be easier, in respect of smaller items, to abuse the statute by dealing in them. Surely the municipalities have, first of all, some conscience and, in the second place, they have to keep records. I would think that one ought to be able to trust them. But in so far as you cannot trust them or if you are not prepared to operate on that basis, it should be remembered that they have records. It surely ought to be possible to have records. If the reason which has been given is the only one, I should like to ask whether the matter could not be reconsidered before this resolution passes. I do not want to be less reasonable than was my colleague the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe.
Carried.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?
No; it is not carried.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall I rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again?

Agreed.
Resolution stands.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: topic
Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, tomorrow and Friday we shall take estimates, beginning with northern affairs, continuing with fisheries and then agriculture.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
